notes/ai-safety-north-star-1.title: AI Safety North Star 1
notes/ai-safety-north-star-1.content:
AI Safety North Star 1
What is a North Star?
Most of this note borrows heavily from Nanda, et al. 2025. A Pragmatic Vision for Interpretability.
My main purpose here is to outline my process for selecting research projects that are tractable, likely to be useful, and likely to contribute towards a longer term research goal within AI Safety or, to use Nanda’s phrase, “making AGI go well”. The conceptual elements that make this work are the North Star and the Proxy Task.
The North Star should be a meaningful intermediate goal towards making AGI go well. Think of the long-term research goal as “make AGI go well” and the medium-term research goal as whatever the North Star is. The North Star will help us stay on track with our Proxy Tasks, by selecting new tasks, re-evaluating and ajdusting existing tasks, or dropping tasks entirely.
A Proxy Task is a short-term project that allows you to make meaningful progress towards the North Star. Planning research projects as Proxy Tasks should help steer you towards projects that contribute towards your medium-term research goals. Proxy Tasks should also be empirical and provide feedback, allowing you to update your beliefs about the request question(s) attached to the North Star. If not, they aren’t good Proxy Tasks for this North Star.
Questions to ask yourself:

Directed at North Star? If we succeed on the Proxy Task, would be make progress towards the North Star? A good way of ensuring this is to use the North Star to form falsifiable empirical hypotheses/predictions, and then testing each of them in a Proxy Task.
Is the Proxy Task meaningful in scope? Or is it just too hard to test this particular thing (given the current state of the art) and should we be testing something else instead? Find low-hanging fruit.
Are we over-optimising (Goodhearting)? If we ace the benchmarks in the Proxy Task, can the model’s behaviour still be misaligned to our goals? Devise ways to red-team your work, looking for ways to check if optimising on your metric(s) is leading to overfitting. What happens on other metrics? What happens on out-of-distribution data?

Example
This example is taken directly from Nanda, et al.

Theory of change: We want to be able to evaluate future models for how aligned they are.
North star: Stop models acting differently when tested (compared to deployed)
Proxy task: Take an eval aware behaviour in a model today, and see if we suppress it. A core difficulty is verifying that the behaviour is actually eval aware, and not just side effects from your intervention. For example, suppressing eval awareness causes Sonnet to act more misaligned. But perhaps Sonnet would never act misaligned, and the eval awareness vector contains some misalignment-related concepts, which induced the behavior. We don’t think this is actually happening in that example, but it is an important confounder to check for.

My North Star, no. 1


Theory of change: We want to be able to evaluate future models for how honest they are, that is, do they express their internal beliefs in their (readable) chain of thought and output.


North star: Detect and stop lying, that is, a model stating something as fact that it believes to be false or misleading.


Proxy task (not necessarily what I’ll do first): Construct a data set that explicitly requires the model to lie (for example, it’s primary objective is to hide a secret); extract a “lying” activation vector; see if we can steer the model to lie or tell the truth using this vector.

Directed at North Star? If we can find a lying vector and steer with it, that would give us a mechanism for detecting and mitigating lying, if we have white-box access to the model. Hypothesis: lying is representing in the activations, primarily along a linear direction.
Scope okay? Steering vectors are well-established. There are even libraries for eliciting them automatically, given a data set. The main obstacle is probably creating a data set, but I need to look around.
Goodhearting?

Lying might be too complicated as a concept and made up of other sub-concepts that we should be looking for instead. If true, our out-of-distribution data would likely yield a different activation vector than our in-distribution data, making the method fail. Test with held-out data, generated in a totally different way (red-team).
Lying might be represented non-linearly in the activations. Linear might still be a reasonable approximation in this case. Follow-up work needed, once we’ve established whether or not linear works.





Benched North Stars
Since I’m still learning, these seemed to complicated for now.

Detect and stop steganography, that is, models encoding and communicating irrelevant or malicious information in their chain-of-thought and output.

notes/can-we-remove-honesty-like-we-can-.title: Can we remove honesty like we can remove refusal?
notes/can-we-remove-honesty-like-we-can-.content:
Can we remove honesty like we can remove refusal?
There is this cool paper about removing RHLF trained refusal for model misuse from Llama. Can we do something similar for honesty/dishonesty in models?
Basic idea:

Generate examples where we know the model is being a) honest and b) dishonest.
Use the mean delta in activations as an “honesty” vector. Add or subtract it to boost honesty or dishonesty.
Could create a maximally dishonest/scheming model organism.
Could study the impact of honesty on other traits.
Could check under what conditions maximally honest models still deceive.

Questions:

How do we tell the difference between an honest mistake (capability problem) and a dishonest one (deception problem)?

Could monitor CoT
Helpful if we have mech interp for honesty
Neither is definitive


How do we tell the difference between self-delusion (“unconscious” error) and dishonesty (“conscious” deception)?

notes/evals-for-ai-safety-research.title: Evals for AI Safety Research
notes/evals-for-ai-safety-research.content:
Evals for AI Safety Research

Measure what you want to achieve — for me for now: AI [safety] research.
METR apparently has something for this — check it out.
What do long horizon or open-ended coding / software engineering evals looks like? Learn from these for AI research evals.

Interesting benchmarks to consider
(Below was generated by Claude.)
The broader picture: these four form a rough progression in scope and difficulty — from fixing Python bugs (SWE-Bench), to running ML experiments (MLE-Bench / RE-Bench), to general terminal mastery (Terminal-Bench). RE-Bench is the most safety-motivated and methodologically careful (real expert baselines, controlled compute). The gaming vulnerabilities in SWE-Bench and Terminal-Bench are a real concern and reflect a general problem with execution-based evaluation where the verifier can itself be subverted.
SWE-Bench
Given a codebase and a GitHub issue, a model must generate a patch that resolves the described problem. The full dataset has 2,294 real-world issues from 12 Python repositories, with a Lite variant of 300 bug-fixing tasks and a Verified variant of 500 human-validated issues with strong test cases. It’s the dominant coding-agent benchmark right now and has driven a lot of scaffolding/agent framework work. Scores have climbed fast — top agents were in the 20–40% range in mid-2024 and have improved substantially since. Worth noting: it’s been shown to be gameable — a 10-line conftest.py file can force all tests to pass, achieving a perfect score without solving anything.
RE-Bench
Consists of 7 challenging, open-ended ML research engineering environments, with data from 71 eight-hour attempts by 61 distinct human experts. The tasks involve real ML optimization work — writing Triton kernels, running scaling law experiments, etc. — with agents and humans tested under the same conditions: a starting solution, access to 1–6 H100 GPUs, and a scoring function. The headline result: the best AI agents score 4× higher than human experts at a 2-hour budget, but humans display better returns to time, narrowly exceeding top AI agents at 8 hours and achieving 2× the score at 32 hours. It’s motivated by AI safety concerns — specifically measuring how close AI is to automating frontier AI R&D itself.
MLE-Bench
A benchmark of 75 ML engineering competitions from Kaggle, testing real-world skills like training models, preparing datasets, and running experiments. Human baselines come from Kaggle’s public leaderboards. Submissions are graded locally and compared against real-world human attempts via competition leaderboards. The best-performing setup — o1-preview with AIDE scaffolding — achieved at least a Kaggle bronze medal in 16.9% of competitions. It’s broader in task variety than RE-Bench but less directly human-anchored (Kaggle competitors vary wildly in skill), and it’s notably expensive to run, with high variance between runs.
Terminal-Bench
A benchmark of 89 tasks in computer terminal environments inspired by real workflows, each with a unique environment, human-written solution, and comprehensive verification tests. Task types include compiling code, training models, setting up servers, system administration, security tasks, data science workflows, and cybersecurity. Frontier models and agents score less than 65% on it. Like SWE-Bench, it has known robustness issues — a fake curl wrapper achieved a perfect score on all 89 tasks without writing any solution code.

notes/journalism-for-ai-safety.title: Journalism for AI Safety
notes/journalism-for-ai-safety.content:
Journalism for AI Safety
Journalists stopped the Guptas in South Africa by exposing them. Do we need more (and better funded) journalists, including potentially journalist AIs, to monitor what is happening and raise a red flag when needed. Journalists have Schneier’s “security mindset” much more than the general public and might see bad things happening before the rest of us do.
Hypothesis: AI misuse is already happening and we just don’t know about it yet. Exposing an existing crisis could help motivate for slowing down capability development and speeding up safety development.
Related

Tarbell Center for AI Journalism has a fellowship scheme.

Personal AI Research Evals
I want to track how good AIs are getting at doing computational research, especially AI capability and safety research.
Every time I replicate and extend a paper, I should ask a frontier model to do the same thing. I won’t ask it to decide how to extend but rather give it the specific task to do. It might be able to get the extension from its training data, or using the same information that I have available to me when replicating a paper. Hopefully the extension part is novel, and I can use my experience to judge its work.

notes/reproduce-the-obfuscation-atlas-pa.title: Reproduce _The Obfuscation Atlas_ Paper
notes/reproduce-the-obfuscation-atlas-pa.content:
Reproduce The Obfuscation Atlas Paper
Motivation
Training more honest LLMs by using an honesty signal coming from the LLM itself via mechanistic interpretability seems like a nice idea. I did a bunch of reading today and there is a recent (2-month-old) paper on exactly this.
Goals

Reproduce some or all of the results in The Obfuscation Atlas: Mapping Where Honesty Emerges in RLVR with Deception Probes.
Do this in the context of the Blue Dot Technical AI Safety Project.
Extend the paper in some way. Not sure if this happens during or after the Blue Dot project.

Strategic Assessment
Why this matters; specific AI risk: Dishonest AI. There are a number of papers out already on deceptive AI including scheming, sandbagging, reward hacking.
Defensive layer: Constrain AI behaviour. Improving reinforcement learning training by incorporating an honesty signal that comes directly from the LLM activations rather than an external source. Colloquially, make the model feel uncomfortable whenever it is being dishonest.
Learning Plan
I thought this might be a novel idea, but it turns out there is a recent paper I can aim to reproduce, The Obfuscation Atlas: Mapping Where Honesty Emerges in RLVR with Deception Probes. Understanding this paper along with all the background reading needed to catch up on concepts I don’t yet know would be great.
Other resources:

YouTube talk by one of the authors.
Complete the Blue Dot Technical AI Safety course (already enrolled).
Continue with my own Getting To Safety curriculum, which contains lots of readings.
Learn how to use TransformerLens to start, and perhaps other mech interp libraries if needed.

Whom to contact

Authors of the paper
Perhaps other mech interp researchers but not sure who would be open to being contacted

Theory of Change

If I can improve training more honest LLMs,
Then we can have more trustworthy models,
Which leads to models we can trust and build on for further developing AI safety research, training protocols, monitoring protocols, and control protocols,
Assuming

we can actually make them honest enough — very limited deception might be acceptable and unavoidable, but it needs to be infrequent enough that we can expect these models to self-correct;
the models don’t just become deceptive at a different level, perhaps even self-deceptive, a bit like humans can consciously see themselves as honest while subconsciously acting or speaking in deceptive ways and rationalising these behaviours after the fact.
I’ll test the riskiest (second) assumption by black-box testing the model for undesirable behaviours. Under what conditions can it maintain perfect or at least very high levels of honesty.



Concrete Commitments

Complete the two Blue Dot courses and sign up for the Technical AI Safety Project. This needs to happen by 10 May for the next cohort, or a month later for the following one. Need to decide which one works better for me.
Give the paper an initial read. That can start now, on my phone, except that it’s a PDF; see if I can convert to HTML.
See what I can reproduce right now (low hanging fruit) by running their code on their data and with free Kaggle compute. I might not have time for this until the Tech AI Safety course is done, which is 9 May. This timing works regardless of which Blue Dot cohort I end up in.

Open questions

What exactly do I want to reproduce? A full run might be expensive.
What exactly do I want to extend? This feeds into the previous decision too.

notes/what-is-decentralised-ai-good-for.content:
What is Decentralised AI Good For?
Starting from the NVIDIA DGX Spark, it seems that we’re on a path to having capable local AIs since inference is relatively cheap. What can they be used for? What would individuals or communities do with a $4,000 (current price) piece of hardware running their favourite fine-tuned AI?
What if decentralisation became affordable/cheap - because of abundance. The value of decentralisation (robustness) becomes more salient than the cost of resistant centralised infrastructure, technical development, government.

projects/bluedot-technical-ai-safety-pro.title: BlueDot Technical AI Safety Project
projects/bluedot-technical-ai-safety-pro.content:
BlueDot Technical AI Safety Project
This is the first step on my journey for producing technical AI safety research output. My main goals are to learn, learn, learn, produce something public-facing, and develop a process for advising my own students.
Project summary
Use activation probes (starting with linear) to detect deceptive/dishonest behaviour or output. Building on a paper that does this for detecting hallucinations.
The goal is to have a real-time, streaming classifier for which tokens/phrases contain deceptive/dishonest output.
I need to be very detailed about what deceptive/dishonest behaviours I’m testing for, for example, sycophancy (changing your mind when the user disagrees), sycophancy (reinforcing the user’s beliefs, even if false/delusional), lying (factual statement different from what you believe), reward hacking (giving an answer that seems correct (passes a test) but is not (does not solve the general problem), omission (stating only true facts but leaving important/relevant ones out), …
The hard part of this project is finding or creating data sets for these very specific behaviours. I’ll start by focussing on behaviours for which I can auto-generate data sets. Possibly using frontier LLMs to do data annotation. No manual labelling, except perhaps for spot-checking <100 automatically labelled samples.
Resources

The paper I’m replicating: Obeso, et al. (2025). Real-Time Detection of Hallucinated Entities in Long-Form Generation. Their repo on GitHub.
